threadTweets:
Base platform: N20 DC motors (200 RPM)

Not the fastest. Not the biggest.

BUT: efficient, reliable, low noise, field-proven in robotics. 6-month runtime on single 18650 charge at typical usage.

We chose runtime over speed.

Head tilt: MG90S servo motor

45g torque. 4.8V nominal. Smooth 90-degree tilt.

Animation possibilities: alert, curious, tired, playful, sleeping.

The head is PawMe's face. It needs to be expressive.

Brain: ESP32-S3

240 MHz dual-core. 8 MB PSRAM. Dual WiFi + Bluetooth.

Open ecosystem. Thousands of libraries. Hardware mature.

We don't need cutting-edge silicon. We need reliability.

Power: 18650 LiPo (3.7V nominal)

2600mAh capacity. 9-10 hour runtime at typical usage.

Wireless charging dock (5W Qi coil) for convenience.

Users can buy spare batteries for $15. No proprietary packs.

Sensors:

Temp (TMP36): Fever detection
Distance (HC-SR04): Obstacle avoidance
IMU (MPU6050): Orientation tracking
Microphone: Voice input
Camera (OV2640): Visual AI

Each sensor independently verified.

mainTweet:
The PawMe firmware stack is completely open-source.

Motor control. IMU processing. Sensor fusion. WiFi AP mode. OTA updates. Voice AI integration.

Here's how the robot brain works 🧵
threadTweets:
Layer 1: Drivers

ESP-IDF HAL handles GPIO, I2C, UART, PWM.

We use raw register writes where speed matters (motor control ISR must be < 1ms).

Arduino compatibility layer for sensor libraries.

Layer 2: Real-time core

Motor PID loop runs at 1kHz via FreeRTOS timer.

IMU fusion estimates orientation every 10ms.

Watchdog ensures crash recovery.

No blocking operations in ISR.

Layer 3: Sensor integration

Temperature sampled every 5 seconds (moving average filter).

Distance sensor triggers obstacle avoidance.

Microphone buffering for 2-second audio chunks.

Camera frame capture on WiFi command.

Layer 4: Cloud integration

WiFi AP mode means user phone connects directly to PawMe (private, no cloud latency).

OpenAI API calls for voice Q&A (optional cloud, can be disabled).

Firmware updates via OTA (encrypted).

Everything is on GitHub. Everything is documented. Everything is MIT licensed.

We learned from Pebby: proprietary firmware = no trust. Open firmware = no surprises.

threadTweets:
Component sourcing priorities:

1000-unit batches: $15-18 per unit (factory assembly)

We're using bonded warehouses to consolidate before final assembly.
